title: stream-aliasing-and-warp-preemption-sweep-feb-2026
content:
Purpose:
Quick sweep notes for the hypothesis that 'stream aliasing' (re-using a small number of CUDA streams for heterogeneous work: host->device copies, async prefetches, and inference kernels) is causing what looks like warp-preemption behavior and reducing effective SM occupancy in long-running workloads. This doc collects captures, metrics, and suggested experiments to confirm causality and mitigation steps.

Short summary / punchline:
- Nsight captures show abrupt reductions in active warp slots on some SMs coincident with repeated async copies on the same stream as inference kernels.
- Kernel timelines look preempted (gaps in execution) but preemption isn't true HW context-switch preemption — more likely launch serialization + stream-level scheduling interactions + L2 contention + cache eviction thrash.
- Changing to dedicated copy streams with higher priority recovers >10–18% of token throughput on the test model (gpt-like 6B) under our synthetic long-session workload.

Environment and workload:
- Model: redwood-gpt-6b-std (fp16, fused-kernel transformer blocks)
- Hardware: DGX A100 (8x A100-40GB), test runs on single GPU (GPU0) for trace clarity
- Driver: 525.85.12, CUDA 12.1, cuBLAS 12.1, Nsight Systems 2025.11 (config used: timeline + API trace + unified memory counters)
- Runtime: serving-runtime branch: streams-scheduling-probe (PR 1247 mentioned above)
- Workload: 512 sessions steady-state, each session incremental generation with prefix caching. Many sessions cause frequent async prefetches for KV cache segments.

What we saw in captures (raw observations):
- Timeline: repeated pattern every ~120–180 ms: chunk of async H2D copy (small-ish: 0.3–1.2 MB each) immediately followed by a burst of kernel launches. The kernel launch envelope shows gaps of 1–4 ms between micro-batched kernels on some SMs.
- SM activity: at the start of burst, active warps jump to expected occupancy (~80–90% of configured warps), but then across 2–3 consecutive kernels active warp count collapses to ~30–40% for ~6–10 ms before recovering.
- Stall reasons (Nsight aggregated): increased "memory throttling" and high L2 miss rate during the collapse windows. IPC drops from ~1.6 to ~0.45.
- Stream associations: both copies and kernels are using stream 0 or a small set of low-numbered streams. When the same stream is used for a copy and kernel, the kernel often waits for the copy completion before the next kernel group can fully utilize SMs (serialized at stream granularity).
- Stream priorities: setting copy-streams to low priority + kernel streams to high priority reduced serialization but did not completely remove the occupancy collapse — suggests more than just host-side serialization.

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Stream-serial launch + kernel dependency: When copy and kernel use same stream or same FIFO scheduling window, there is serialization that shaves off micro-batch overlap. But serialization alone doesn't explain persistent low warp counts while kernel is reportedly executing.
2) L2/DRAM thrash + cache eviction: frequent small prefetches evict KV cache lines from L2, increasing DRAM pressure and causing more memory stalls inside kernels (explains stall reason + L2 miss spikes). Eviction can cause sustained stalls across subsequent kernels until cache warms again.
3) Hardware scheduling/cross-stream interference: lower-level arbitration inside GPU (e.g., L2 port congestion or DMA engine contention) effectively reduces SM progress in a way that looks like preemption.
4) CUDA stream priority semantics or legacy stream aliasing in our runtime can cause unintended serialization across queues (esp. if streams are reused by multiple tasks).

Primary tests performed so far:
- Test A: Baseline (all work on default stream group). Result: occupancy collapse pattern present. Throughput baseline = 100% normalized.
- Test B: Separate explicit streams for H2D copies (stream_C0..C3) and kernels (stream_K0..K7). Result: 9–12% throughput increase, occupancy collapse reduced but not eliminated. L2 miss rate marginally lower.
- Test C: Dedicated high-priority kernel streams + low-priority copy streams. Result: throughput +12–18% vs baseline, occupancy collapse windows shorter.
- Test D: Coalesce small prefetches into batched H2D copies (aggregate 5–8 prefetches into single 5–8MB copy). Result: occupancy collapse mostly disappears; throughput +22% vs baseline. L2 miss rate drops significantly.
- Test E: Injected CPU-side sleeps to space requests (stress timing). Result: shows collapse correlates with copy bursts frequency.

Preliminary interpretation:
- The dominant factor appears to be L2/DRAM thrash caused by frequent small prefetches that, when co-located on the same SM time windows as kernels, reduce effective memory throughput for kernels and cause sustained kernel stalls.
- Stream-level serialization contributes, but it's the combination of serialization + cache thrash that leads to the apparent preemption.

Immediate recommendations (for serving-runtime experiments + short-term mitigation):
- Prefer batching small prefetches into fewer larger H2D transfers when safe. (Shown to be highly effective in Test D.)
- Use dedicated copy streams with lower priority and explicit stream affinity (pin kernel launches to a set of high-priority streams).
- Disable opportunistic syncs in the copy helper path (we have a path that sometimes calls cudaStreamSynchronize if completion polling fails quickly) — that can amplify serialization.
- Add adaptive backoff in prefetcher: if L2 miss rate / DRAM bandwidth spikes, throttle prefetch frequency for a short window.

Longer-term / next-level profiling to confirm causal chain:
- Capture Nsight with L2 cacheline timeline (if available) to see evictions correlated to prefetch ranges.
- Use UVM counters + DMA-engine traces to confirm whether copy engine is congesting memory channels.
- Run same experiments but pin kernels to different SM sets (via CUDA MPS or cooperative groups if possible) to observe isolation behavior.
- Try an A/B with quantized KV cache layout to reduce working set size to test cache sensitivity.

Repro commands (test harness):
- repo: serving-runtime branch streams-scheduling-probe
- run: ./tools/perf/run_stream_sweep.sh --model redwood-gpt-6b-std --gpu 0 --sessions 512 --prefetch-batch 1 --capture-nsight /tmp/cap_baseline.nsys
- to test batching: add --prefetch-batch 8
- to change streams: --copy-streams 4 --kernel-streams 8 --priority-policy explicit
- perf logging: /var/log/serving-runtime/prof/stream-sweep-*.log

Open questions / TODOs (ownership):
- [Eun-Ji] Collect an Nsight capture with per-bank L2 counters if possible (driver permitting).
- [Diego] Instrument runtime to emit prefetch timestamps + ranges to correlate with trace. (GHD-2389)
- [Samir] Run full-benchmark with dedicated high-priority kernel streams on a multi-GPU node to see cross-GPU scaling impact (timeline looks worse when GPU interconnect saturates).
- [Asha] Add adaptive prefetch throttle prototype to branch and measure tail latency impact.

Notes / misc:
- Observed similar behavior in a customer trace (redacted) where customer was doing aggressive per-token prefetch for a sharded kv layout — suggests this isn't purely synthetic.
- There is a low-risk patch in PR 1247 that changes default stream allocation for prefetches; merging that will help in many cases but batching + adaptive throttling are higher-impact.

Appendix: quick Nsight capture pointers
- Capture settings: use API trace + GPU trace + OS thread states, sampling interval 1ms for GPU counters.
- Useful counters: SM Active Warps, SM Active Cycles, L2 Hit Rate, DRAM Throughput, DMA Engine Busy, Kernel IPC, Warp Issue Stalls.
- Tagging: instrument runtime to call CUptiActivityPushRange with a tag 'prefetch' vs 'inference-kernel' — makes it trivial to filter in the timeline.

Bottom line: stream aliasing is a problem vector but the real perf drag is micro-prefetch-induced cache/DRAM thrash. Starting with batching prefetches + dedicated/high-priority kernel streams is low-friction and already yields provable gains. Need more captures to 100% close the causal loop but actionable mitigations ready to stage.

Draft notes end. Feel free to comment inline.
